newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr extends overnight losses but off lows in Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Dlr extends overnight losses but off lows in Tokyo.

text.p: 0611 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0600 GMT

The dollar extended overnight losses against the yen but was off lows by late Tokyo on Tuesday as bids near 114 yen and speculation of a weak "tankan" survey by the Bank of Japan kept its downside solid.
Dealers said overnight comments by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Japan's holdings of U.S. Treasuries had little lasting impact on currencies in Tokyo.

Hashimoto on Monday urged U.S. cooperation on stabilising foreing exchange rates, saying currency volatility might cause the Japanese government to sell holdings of U.S. government securities and switch funds to gold.
"I hope the U.S. will engage in efforts and in cooperation to maintain exchange stability so we will not succumb to the temptation to sell off Treasury bills and switch our funds to gold," he said.
But dealers in Tokyo said they believed it was unrealistic to think the Japanese government would sell U.S. Treasury bills and therefore the impact of the remarks was short-lived.

Japan's Finance Ministry said in a statement issued on Tuesday that Japan would continue to cooperate with the United States to stabilise foreign exchange rates and that Hashimoto regretted that his intentions had not been accurately conveyed.
"I think he made the comments accidentally without political incentives," said a senior dealer at a U.S. bank.

Another dealer at a trust bank said: "His comments came out when traders began to feel U.S. stocks and bonds have recently been overheated. And the dollar was sold in tandem with falls in U.S. stocks and bonds overnight."
He added that the market is now watching how U.S. stocks and bonds will fare later in overseas trade.
Japanese trust banks, probably on behalf of pension funds, were said to be major buyers of dollars for yen near 114 yen, limiting the dollar's fall, dealers said.

The market widely expects that the Bank of Japan's quarterly "tankan" survey due out at 8.50 a.m. Wednesday (2350 GMT Tuesday) will show weak business sentiment, which also supported the dollar's downside. But a city bank dealer said that as speculation of a weak tankan has been already factored into the market, the impact on currencies may be limited.
"We will focus more on ascertaining when Japan will raise its interest rates (by looking at forecasts for next quarter), rather than weak results in the current quarter," he added.

On the topside, U.S. securities houses sold dollars for yen, which encouraged other traders to unload their dollar long positions, dealers said. Sporadic exporter offers above 115 yen also capped the greenback's gains, they said.

Dealers said stop-loss sales may emerge near and below 114 yen, keeping downside risk intact. A dealer in Singapore predicted that the yen could open between 113.25 and 113.50 yen on Wednesday ahead of the tankan release.
Japanese government bond futures and euroyen futures received a boost partly on expectations of a poor tankan report, but dealers said the impact on currencies was limited.

The dollar was directionless against the mark, while the mark edged down against the yen by late Tokyo after hitting recent highs of around 67.12 yen overnight. The German currency stood near 66.43/46 yen at 0658 GMT, down from 66.80 yen in late New York on Monday.
The dollar closed at 114.71/76 yen and 1.7170/80 marks in New York on Monday. -- Singapore newsroom +65-8703080, Yoko Nishikawa in Tokyo +81-3-3432-8584
